p: Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight we walk out of the counting house and into the open air, for geometry means, in Greek, the measuring of the earth. The Egyptians, so Herodotus tells us, needed it to remeasure their fields after the Nile flooded each year. Since we are working by ear, I shall describe shapes as one might describe a walk, and I encourage you to trace them with a finger in the air, or on the arm of your chair, as I speak.
## Points and lines

Euclid's Elements, written in Alexandria about three hundred years before Christ, begins with definitions. A point is that which has no part: it marks a position, but has no size at all. A line has length but no breadth.

In modern language, a line goes on for ever in both directions. A piece of a line with two ends is called a line segment, and one with a single end, going on for ever in the other direction, is called a ray, like a ray of light from a lamp.
My cat, I should say, is named after Euclid, because he too has a great deal of position and, in his own estimation, no faults at all.
## Angles

When two lines meet, they make an angle, which measures how far you would turn to face along one line instead of the other. Imagine standing at a crossroads facing north. Turn to face east: that is a quarter turn, called a right angle. Keep turning to face south: half a turn, a straight line. All the way round to face north again: a full turn.
We measure angles in degrees. A full turn is three hundred and sixty degrees.

Why three hundred and sixty? Most probably it comes down to us from the Babylonians, who counted in sixties, as you heard in an earlier lecture, and from the year having roughly three hundred and sixty days. Three hundred and sixty is also a splendid number to divide: by two, three, four, five, six, eight, nine, ten, twelve and many more.
Half a turn, a straight line, is a hundred and eighty degrees. A quarter turn, a right angle, is ninety degrees. Like the corner of a page.
?? While I pour. How many degrees in three quarters of a turn?
=> Two hundred and seventy degrees.

An angle smaller than a right angle is called acute, meaning sharp, like the point of a pencil. Between ninety and a hundred and eighty is obtuse, meaning blunt. More than a hundred and eighty is a reflex angle, bending back on itself.
## Angles on a line
If two angles sit side by side on a straight line, together they make half a turn, so they add up to a hundred and eighty degrees. If one is a hundred and ten, the other must be seventy.

When two straight lines cross, like an X, the angles opposite each other are equal. They are called vertically opposite angles. Picture a pair of scissors slightly open: the angle between the blades equals the angle between the handles.
## Parallel lines

Two lines in a flat surface that never meet, however far they go, are called parallel, like the rails of a railway line. When another line crosses two parallel lines, it makes the same angles with each. Euclid's famous fifth postulate is about parallel lines, and it proved so troublesome that in the nineteenth century mathematicians discovered whole geometries in which it fails, but that is a story for a lecture on bigger ideas. Euclid the cat, as I have said, has no views on parallel lines whatever.
## Triangles
A triangle has three straight sides and three angles. And here is a fact to treasure: the three angles of any triangle, whatever its shape, add up to a hundred and eighty degrees.
⟦x+y+z=180^\circ⟧

You can see why with a paper triangle. Tear off the three corners and put them side by side: they make a straight line. Or imagine walking around the triangle. At each corner you turn, and by the time you return to the start you have turned a full turn, three hundred and sixty degrees. The turns at the corners are the outside angles; each inside angle is a hundred and eighty minus its turn. Three corners give five hundred and forty, minus three hundred and sixty: a hundred and eighty. A walk in the park proves a theorem.
?? A triangle has angles of fifty and sixty degrees. What is the third?
=> Fifty plus sixty is a hundred and ten. A hundred and eighty minus a hundred and ten is seventy degrees.

Triangles have names. Equilateral: all three sides equal, and all three angles sixty degrees. Isosceles, which in Greek means equal legs: two sides equal, and the two angles opposite them equal. Scalene: all sides different. And a right-angled triangle has one angle of ninety degrees. That one will bring us Pythagoras.
## More sides

A four-sided shape is a quadrilateral. Draw a diagonal and it splits into two triangles, so its angles add up to two hundred and sixty, no, I beg your pardon, two times a hundred and eighty, three hundred and sixty. You see, even professors must check their arithmetic, and Mrs Blewitt would have caught that before I opened my mouth.
Squares, rectangles, parallelograms, rhombuses, kites and trapeziums are all quadrilaterals. A shape with five sides is a pentagon, six a hexagon, like the cells of a honeycomb, and eight an octagon.
?? A five-sided shape can be cut into three triangles. What do its angles add up to?
=> Three times a hundred and eighty, five hundred and forty degrees.
## Summary

A point has position but no size; lines go on for ever; segments have ends. Angles measure turning: three hundred and sixty for a full turn, a hundred and eighty for a straight line, ninety for a right angle. Angles on a line make a hundred and eighty, and so do the angles in a triangle. Quadrilaterals make three hundred and sixty. Next time: perimeter and area, or fencing and turf. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight the most famous theorem in all mathematics, the one that every schoolchild meets and many adults still half remember. It is named after Pythagoras, though, as you will hear, he was far from the first to know it. And I shall prove it to you without a single drawing, by asking you to imagine some tiles.
## The theorem
Take a right-angled triangle. The longest side, opposite the right angle, is called the hypotenuse, from the Greek for stretching under. Call the two shorter sides a and b, and the hypotenuse c.

In plain words: the square of one short side, plus the square of the other, equals the square of the hypotenuse. Euclid said it in terms of actual squares: the square built on the hypotenuse has the same area as the two squares built on the other sides put together.
## The famous example
The sides three, four and five.

Nine plus sixteen is twenty-five. It balances. A triangle with sides three, four and five, in any units, must have a right angle. There is a pretty story that Egyptian surveyors, called rope stretchers, used a loop of rope knotted into twelve equal spaces to make right angles for their buildings. I must tell you honestly that historians regard this as an attractive guess rather than an established fact.
?? While I pour. A right-angled triangle has short sides six and eight. What is the hypotenuse?
=> Six squared is thirty-six, eight squared is sixty-four, together a hundred. The square root of a hundred is ten.
## Finding a shorter side
If you know the hypotenuse and one short side, subtract instead. A ladder thirteen feet long leans against a wall with its foot five feet from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach?
The square root of a hundred and forty-four is twelve. Twelve feet up the wall. Five, twelve, thirteen is another of these happy whole-number triangles, called Pythagorean triples.
?? A rope ten yards long is stretched from the top of a pole to a peg in the ground six yards from the pole's foot. How tall is the pole?
=> Ten squared is a hundred, six squared thirty-six. A hundred minus thirty-six is sixty-four, and its square root is eight. Eight yards.
## A proof with tiles

Now, why is it true? Imagine a large square floor, with each side of length a plus b. In it, I place four identical copies of our right-angled triangle, one in each corner, each with its right angle in a corner of the floor and its short sides along the edges. The hypotenuses face inwards, and between them they enclose a tilted square, with side c. Its area is c squared.

Now rearrange the same four triangles on the same floor: push them together in pairs, so that each pair makes a rectangle a by b, and put the two rectangles in opposite corners. Now the uncovered floor is two squares: one a by a, and one b by b. Their total area is a squared plus b squared.

Same floor, same four triangles, so the uncovered parts must be equal. c squared equals a squared plus b squared. No algebra required at all. This proof, or one like it, is very old; versions are associated with ancient Chinese mathematics.
## Who knew it first?

A Babylonian clay tablet called Plimpton 322, from about eighteen hundred years before Christ, lists numbers that most historians read as Pythagorean triples, some of them quite large, such as a hundred and nineteen, a hundred and twenty and a hundred and sixty-nine. That was over a thousand years before Pythagoras. The ancient Chinese text called the Zhoubi Suanjing discusses the same relation. Ancient Indian builders of altars knew it too.

Pythagoras himself lived around five hundred and seventy to four hundred and ninety-five years before Christ and led a brotherhood in southern Italy that mixed mathematics, music and mysticism, including, it is said, a refusal to eat beans. We have no writings by Pythagoras himself, and no one knows whether he proved the theorem. The tale that he sacrificed an ox in celebration is a later story, and an odd one for a man who is also said to have been a vegetarian.
## A proof by a future President

My favourite modern proof was published in 1876 by James Garfield, then a member of the American Congress and later, briefly, President of the United States. He used a trapezium made of two copies of the triangle and a half square, and compared areas. That an American politician found time to prove a theorem has always struck me as a most encouraging sign for democracy.
## Distance between two points

Pythagoras also measures straight-line distances. Walk three streets east and four streets north. How far are you, as the crow flies, from where you started? Five streets. On a map with coordinates, the distance between two points is found by making a right-angled triangle from the east-west gap and the north-south gap.
## The converse

The theorem works backwards too. If a squared plus b squared equals c squared, the triangle has a right angle. That is how builders check corners are square: measure three along one wall, four along the other, and the diagonal should be exactly five.
## Summary

In a right-angled triangle, a squared plus b squared equals c squared, with c the hypotenuse. Add squares to find the hypotenuse; subtract to find a shorter side. Triples like three, four, five and five, twelve, thirteen give whole numbers. The Babylonians knew it long before Pythagoras. Next time, circles and the number pi. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight we meet the most famous number after one and nought: pi. It is the number every circle carries in its pocket, and it has fascinated, and sometimes driven quite mad, mathematicians and amateurs for four thousand years.
## The words of the circle

The centre is the middle point. The radius is the distance from the centre to the edge, like a spoke of a cartwheel. The diameter goes right across through the centre: two radii, end to end. The circumference is the distance all the way round, the circle's perimeter.
## What pi is

Take any circle: a cartwheel, a penny, a dinner plate. Measure round it, and measure across it. Divide the first by the second. You always get the same number, a little more than three. That number is pi.
⟦\pi=\frac{C}{d}\approx 3.14159⟧
In plain words: pi is the circumference over the diameter, approximately three point one four one five nine. So the distance round any circle is a bit more than three times the distance across.
?? While I pour. A cartwheel is one yard across. Roughly how far does it roll in one turn?
=> About three point one four yards, a little more than three.
## Formulas
⟦C=\pi d=2\pi r⟧
The circumference is pi times the diameter, or two pi times the radius, since the diameter is twice the radius.
The area is pi times the radius squared. Notice: the radius, not the diameter, and squared, because area is two-dimensional.
?? A circular pond has a radius of ten feet. Taking pi as about three, roughly what is its area?
=> Ten squared is a hundred, times three is about three hundred square feet. More precisely, three hundred and fourteen.
## Why pi r squared?

Here is a lovely argument. Cut a circle into many thin slices, like a pie. Lay them in a row, alternately point up and point down, so they interlock. The result looks like a rough rectangle with wavy top and bottom. The more slices, the straighter the edges. The height of the rectangle is the radius. Its length is half the circumference, since half the crust is on top and half on the bottom: half of two pi r, which is pi r. Area: pi r times r, which is pi r squared.
Making the slices thinner and thinner until the shape becomes exactly a rectangle is the idea of a limit, which we shall meet properly at the summit.
## Archimedes and the polygons

Archimedes of Syracuse, about two hundred and fifty years before Christ, pinned pi down by trapping the circle between polygons: one drawn inside it and one outside. With polygons of ninety-six sides, he showed that pi lies between three and ten seventy-firsts and three and one seventh.

In plain words: pi is more than two hundred and twenty-three seventy-firsts and less than twenty-two sevenths. That is between about three point one four zero eight and three point one four two nine. Twenty-two sevenths, his upper bound, is still a handy schoolroom value. And he did it without decimals, without algebra, and without the number pi having a name.
## The name

The Greek letter pi was first used for this number by a Welsh mathematician, William Jones, in 1706. It was Leonhard Euler, using it in his widely read books from the 1730s onwards, who made it standard. Pi is the first letter of the Greek words for periphery and perimeter.
## The digits go on for ever

Pi is irrational: its decimal never ends and never repeats. Johann Lambert proved this in 1761. Then, in 1882, Ferdinand von Lindemann proved something stronger: pi is transcendental, which means it is not the solution of any ordinary polynomial equation with whole-number coefficients. That settled an ancient puzzle. The Greeks had asked whether one could construct, with only a straight edge and compasses, a square with exactly the same area as a given circle: squaring the circle. Lindemann's proof shows it is impossible. Augustus De Morgan, who catalogued circle-squarers in his Budget of Paradoxes, would have been delighted, though he did not live to see it.
## Mr Shanks

In 1873 an English schoolmaster named William Shanks published pi to seven hundred and seven decimal places, calculated by hand over many years. It was a heroic labour. Alas, the library of the future informs me that in 1944 it was found that he had made an error at the five hundred and twenty-eighth place, and every digit after was wrong. I tell you this not to mock Mr Shanks, whom I admire enormously, but to show why Mr Babbage wanted his engines. Machines have since calculated trillions of digits.
## Summary

Pi is the circumference divided by the diameter of any circle, about three point one four one five nine. Circumference is two pi r; area is pi r squared, which a pie cut into slices makes plausible. Archimedes trapped pi between polygons; William Jones named it in 1706; it is irrational and transcendental, so the circle cannot be squared. Next time, volume: filling boxes, tins and spheres. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight we climb the last slope of geometry before the ridge. Trigonometry means triangle measuring, and it is the art of finding lengths from angles, and angles from lengths. It is how surveyors mapped India, how navigators found their way across oceans, and, through the library of the future, I learn that it lives inside every sound your little glass slate makes. But we begin with a single triangle.
## The idea

Last time we learnt that triangles with the same angles are similar: their sides are in proportion. So in every right-angled triangle with, say, a thirty-degree angle, the ratio of any two sides is the same, however large or small the triangle. Those fixed ratios are the trigonometric ratios. Each angle carries its own set, like a fingerprint.
## Naming the sides

Pick one of the two smaller angles in a right-angled triangle, and stand at its corner. The hypotenuse, as always, is the longest side, opposite the right angle. The side across the triangle from you, not touching your corner, is the opposite. The remaining side, which runs from your corner to the right angle, is the adjacent, meaning lying next to.
The names depend on which angle you stand at. Walk to the other corner, and opposite and adjacent swap.
## The three ratios
$$ \sin\theta=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}
The sine of the angle, which we call theta, is the opposite over the hypotenuse.
$$ \cos\theta=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}
The cosine is the adjacent over the hypotenuse.
$$ \tan\theta=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}
The tangent is the opposite over the adjacent.

The memory aid is SOH CAH TOA. Sine, opposite, hypotenuse. Cosine, adjacent, hypotenuse. Tangent, opposite, adjacent. Say it like the name of a distant island: SOH CAH TOA. Generations of children have chanted it. I suspect it is more recent than my own schooldays, but it is a good one.
?? While I pour. In a right-angled triangle, the side opposite an angle is five and the hypotenuse is ten. What is the sine of that angle?
=> Five over ten, one half. That angle, as it happens, is thirty degrees.
## Some special angles
A few angles have tidy values worth knowing.
⟦\sin 30^\circ=\frac{1}{2}⟧

The sine of thirty degrees is one half. Picture an equilateral triangle with sides of two, cut in half down the middle: you get a right-angled triangle with a hypotenuse of two and a short side of one opposite the thirty-degree angle.
⟦\tan 45^\circ=1⟧
The tangent of forty-five degrees is one. A right-angled triangle with a forty-five degree angle has two equal short sides, so opposite over adjacent is one.
For other angles, people used printed tables, and now use calculators.
## Finding a length

You stand forty yards from the foot of a church tower, and the angle from the ground up to the top is fifty degrees. How tall is the tower? You know the adjacent, forty, and want the opposite. Opposite and adjacent: TOA, tangent.
⟦h=40\tan 50^\circ⟧
The tangent of fifty degrees is about one point one nine. Forty times that is about forty-eight yards. You have measured a tower without climbing it.
?? A ladder ten feet long makes an angle of sixty degrees with the ground. The cosine of sixty degrees is one half. How far is its foot from the wall?
=> The ladder is the hypotenuse and the distance to the wall is adjacent: CAH. Ten times one half is five feet.
## Finding an angle

Run it backwards. A ramp rises one foot over a horizontal distance of twelve feet. What angle does it make? Opposite over adjacent is one twelfth, so the tangent of the angle is one twelfth. The inverse tangent, written tan to the minus one, gives the angle: about four point eight degrees. Inverse here means undo, just as with functions, which we shall meet shortly.
## A curious word

Why sine? The story is a chain of translations, and it is reasonably well documented. Indian astronomers used a half-chord called jya. Arabic scholars wrote it as jiba, and since Arabic is often written without vowels, a later reader took it as jaib, meaning a fold or a pocket. Twelfth-century translators into Latin rendered that as sinus, a fold or bay. And so sine is, quite literally, a mistranslation. Mrs Blewitt says this is what comes of not checking one's sums.
## History

The Greek astronomer Hipparchus, in the second century before Christ, made a table of chords for astronomy, and Ptolemy's Almagest extended it. Indian mathematicians, especially Aryabhata around five hundred after Christ, developed sines much as we have them. Islamic mathematicians added the tangent and much more.
## Summary

In a right-angled triangle, label the hypotenuse, the opposite and the adjacent from the angle you care about. Sine is opposite over hypotenuse, cosine adjacent over hypotenuse, tangent opposite over adjacent: SOH CAH TOA. Use them to find heights and distances, and the inverse functions to find angles. Next we reach the ridge: graphs and functions. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight two practical questions that every farmer, builder and housekeeper asks. How much fence do I need to go round my field? That is perimeter. And how much turf, or carpet, or paint, do I need to cover it? That is area. People confuse them constantly, and the confusion has cost many a careless builder his profit.
## Perimeter

The perimeter is the total distance around the edge. From the Greek, peri, around, and metron, measure. For a rectangle twelve feet by ten feet, walk around it: twelve, ten, twelve, ten. Forty-four feet.
In plain words: twice the length plus twice the width.
?? While I pour. What is the perimeter of a square with sides of seven yards?
=> Four sevens, twenty-eight yards.
## Area and square units

Area measures surface. We measure it by counting squares. A square foot is a square one foot on each side. A rectangle three feet by two feet can be cut into two rows of three square feet: six square feet.
⟦A=lw⟧

In plain words: area is length times width. The twelve by ten room has an area of a hundred and twenty square feet. Notice the units: square feet, not feet. Perimeter is a length; area is a surface. Mixing them is like asking how many pints are in a mile.
## A warning about scaling

Here is a lovely surprise. Double the sides of a square, from three to six. The perimeter doubles, from twelve to twenty-four. But the area goes from nine to thirty-six: four times as much. When lengths double, areas quadruple, because area grows in two directions at once. This is why a lady's tablecloth twice the size of her old one needs four times the linen, as Mrs Blewitt found out to her cost at the draper's.
?? If every length of a carpet is tripled, how many times more carpet is needed?
=> Three times three, nine times as much.
## Triangles
Take a rectangle and draw a diagonal. It splits into two equal triangles. So a right-angled triangle has half the area of its rectangle.
⟦A=\frac{1}{2}bh⟧

In plain words: half the base times the height. And this works for every triangle, not just right-angled ones, provided the height is measured straight up from the base at a right angle. This is called the perpendicular height: the distance a plumb line would hang from the top corner down to the base, or to the base extended.

Why does it work for any triangle? Imagine the triangle inside a rectangle with the same base and height. The top corner splits the rectangle into two parts, and in each part the triangle takes exactly half. Half plus half of the pieces is half the whole.
?? A triangle has a base of ten metres and a height of six. Its area?
=> Ten times six is sixty, and half of that is thirty square metres.
## Parallelograms

A parallelogram is a rectangle that has been pushed sideways, like a deck of cards nudged at the top. Its area is base times perpendicular height, not base times slanting side. Cut the triangle off one end and slide it to the other: it becomes a rectangle with the same base and height.
⟦A=bh⟧
## Trapeziums
A trapezium has one pair of parallel sides, of different lengths, like a slice through a lampshade. Its area is the average of the two parallel sides, times the height.
⟦A=\frac{(a+b)h}{2}⟧
In plain words: add the two parallel sides, multiply by the height, and halve. If the parallel sides are six and ten, and the height four: sixteen times four is sixty-four, halved is thirty-two.
## Compound shapes

An L-shaped room is just two rectangles stuck together. Cut it with an imaginary line, find each area, and add. Most real shapes yield to this: cut into rectangles and triangles, then sum. In calculus, at the summit of our mountain, we shall do exactly this with infinitely many infinitely thin strips, to find the areas of curved shapes. Hold on to the idea.
## Old measures

In my day, land was measured in acres. An acre was originally the land a team of oxen could plough in a day, and was fixed at a strip a furlong long and a chain wide: two hundred and twenty yards by twenty-two yards, which is four thousand eight hundred and forty square yards. The chain, twenty-two yards, is still the length of a cricket pitch.
## Summary

Perimeter is distance around; area is surface inside, in square units. Rectangle: length times width. Triangle: half base times perpendicular height. Parallelogram: base times height. Trapezium: average of parallel sides times height. Doubling lengths quadruples area. Next time, the most famous theorem of all: Pythagoras. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Perimeter was the fence; area was the turf. Tonight, the third dimension: volume, the amount of space inside a thing. How much tea will the caddy hold? How much water in the cistern? How much coal in the cellar? Mrs Blewitt asks the last question every October.
## Cubic units

Volume is measured in cubes. A cubic inch is a cube one inch along each edge, a little smaller than a sugar lump. A box three inches long, two wide and two high can be filled with layers of cubes: each layer holds three times two, six cubes, and there are two layers. Twelve cubic inches.
⟦V=lwh⟧

In plain words: length times width times height. A cistern four feet by three feet by two feet holds twenty-four cubic feet of water. A cubic foot of water weighs a little over sixty-two pounds, so that cistern holds some two-thirds of a ton. I recommend a strong floor.
?? While I pour. What is the volume of a cube with edges of five centimetres?
=> Five times five times five, a hundred and twenty-five cubic centimetres.
## Scaling again

Last time we saw that doubling lengths quadruples area. For volume it is more dramatic: double every length, and the volume grows by two times two times two, eight times. Triple, and it grows twenty-seven times.

This is why giants in stories could not exist as simply enlarged humans. Galileo pointed this out in 1638. Make a man ten times taller, and his weight, which goes with volume, grows a thousand times, but the strength of his bones, which goes with the area of their cross-section, grows only a hundred times. His legs would break. It is also why a mouse can fall a long way unharmed and an elephant cannot. And why Euclid the cat, being large, prefers to descend from the dresser by way of my lap.
## Prisms and cylinders

A prism is a shape with the same cross-section all the way along, like a stick of seaside rock, a length of timber, or a loaf of bread before slicing. Its volume is the area of the cross-section times the length.
A cylinder, like a tin of peas, is a prism with a circular cross-section. The area of the circle is pi r squared, so:
In plain words: pi times the radius squared times the height.
?? A tin has a radius of two inches and a height of five. Taking pi as about three, roughly what is its volume?
=> Two squared is four, times three is twelve, times five is sixty cubic inches. More precisely, about sixty-three.
## Cones and pyramids
A cone, like an ice-cream cornet or a dunce's cap, or a pyramid, comes to a point. Its volume is exactly one third of the prism with the same base and height.

The one third is surprising. You can test it in the kitchen: fill a cone with water three times, and it fills the matching cylinder. The ancient Egyptians knew how to find the volume of a pyramid, and of a cut-off pyramid, as shown in the Moscow papyrus from nearly four thousand years ago. Eudoxus of Cnidus gave the first rigorous proof of the one third, and Archimedes credited him.
## The sphere
The volume of a ball, a sphere of radius r, is:
In plain words: four thirds pi r cubed. Cubed, notice, because volume is three-dimensional.

Archimedes discovered this, and something more beautiful. Put a sphere snugly inside a cylinder that just encloses it. The sphere has exactly two thirds of the volume of the cylinder, and, remarkably, two thirds of its surface area too. Archimedes was so proud of this that he asked for a sphere in a cylinder to be carved on his tomb. And here is history I can vouch for, because the man tells it himself: Cicero, when he was a Roman official in Sicily in 75 before Christ, searched for the forgotten tomb and found it, overgrown with brambles, recognising it by that very carving.
?? Roughly what is the volume of a sphere of radius three? Take pi as about three.
=> Three cubed is twenty-seven. Four thirds of three is four, and four times twenty-seven is a hundred and eight.
## Eureka, perhaps

The best-known story of Archimedes is that he noticed his bath overflow, realised that the volume of water displaced equals the volume of his body, and ran naked through Syracuse crying Eureka, I have found it. The story comes from the Roman architect Vitruvius, writing about two centuries later, and I would not swear to it in court. But the principle, that you can measure the volume of an awkward object by how much water it pushes aside, is perfectly sound, and Mrs Blewitt uses it to measure her pudding basins.
## Litres and gallons

A litre is a thousand cubic centimetres, a cube ten centimetres on each side. An imperial gallon, defined in 1824, was the volume of ten pounds of water, about four and a half litres. A pint is an eighth of a gallon. Mrs Blewitt measures in pints; my library ticket informs me that you measure in litres, except, I gather, for milk and beer.
## Summary

Volume measures space in cubic units. A box is length times width times height. Prisms and cylinders are cross-section times length: pi r squared h. Cones and pyramids are one third of that. A sphere is four thirds pi r cubed. Double the lengths and the volume grows eight times. Next time, similar triangles: how Thales measured a pyramid with a stick. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight a lecture with an old story in it, a practical trick for measuring things you cannot reach, and the foundation on which all of trigonometry will be built next time.
## Same shape, different size

Two shapes are similar when one is an exact enlargement of the other: the same shape, but perhaps a different size. A photograph and its enlargement are similar. A map and the land it shows are, ideally, similar. Similar shapes have exactly the same angles, and all their lengths are multiplied by the same number, called the scale factor.
If a map has a scale of one to ten thousand, every length on the ground is ten thousand times the length on the map. One centimetre on the map is a hundred metres on the ground.
?? While I pour. On a map at a scale of one to fifty thousand, how many kilometres does two centimetres represent?
=> Two centimetres times fifty thousand is a hundred thousand centimetres: one kilometre.
## Triangles are special

For most shapes, equal angles are not enough to make them similar. A square and a long thin rectangle both have four right angles, but they are not the same shape. Triangles are different. If two triangles have the same three angles, they are guaranteed to be similar: their sides are in proportion.
In fact, two equal angles suffice, because the third must then match too, since all three add up to a hundred and eighty degrees.
## Thales and the pyramid

The story goes, and it is told by ancient writers long after the event, so treat it as a legend, that Thales of Miletus, often called the first Greek mathematician, measured the height of the Great Pyramid of Egypt by its shadow.

He planted a stick upright in the sand. At the moment when the stick's shadow was exactly as long as the stick was tall, the pyramid's shadow, measured from the centre of its base, must also have equalled the pyramid's height. Why? The sun's rays strike both at the same angle, so the stick and its shadow, and the pyramid and its shadow, form similar triangles.
You do not even need to wait for that special moment. Any time will do, if you use proportion.

A stick two metres tall casts a shadow three metres long. At the same moment a tree casts a shadow thirty metres long. The tree's height over its shadow equals the stick's height over its shadow. Thirty is ten times three, so the tree is ten times two: twenty metres.
?? A post one metre high casts a shadow of one and a half metres. A church tower casts a shadow of sixty metres. How tall is the tower?
=> Sixty is forty times one and a half, so the tower is forty times one metre: forty metres.
## Finding a missing side

In general: two similar triangles, one with sides three, four, five and a larger one with its shortest side six. The scale factor is six divided by three, two. So the other sides are eight and ten. Always find the scale factor first, by dividing a pair of matching sides, then multiply.
## Areas and volumes scale differently
You heard in the last two lectures that areas and volumes do not scale like lengths. With similar shapes and a scale factor k:
⟦\text{lengths}\times k,\ \text{areas}\times k^{2},\ \text{volumes}\times k^{3}⟧

In plain words: lengths are multiplied by k, areas by k squared, volumes by k cubed. A model ship at a scale of one to a hundred has a hull area one ten-thousandth of the real ship's, and holds one millionth of its volume. So a model ship full of tea would barely fill a thimble.
?? Two similar jugs: one is twice as tall as the other. How many times more does the big one hold?
=> Two cubed, eight times as much.
## Surveying

Similar triangles were the working tool of surveyors for centuries. In my own lifetime, the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, begun in 1802, measured the subcontinent with chains of triangles across thousands of miles, using careful measurement of one base line and then angles alone. It was directed for many years by Sir George Everest, and in the 1850s its computers established that a mountain known as Peak Fifteen was the highest in the world. It was named after him. The same trick, of measuring angles rather than distances, is what we shall study next time, under the name trigonometry.
## Summary

Similar shapes are enlargements: equal angles, sides in proportion. For triangles, equal angles guarantee similarity. Shadows and sticks measure heights, as Thales is said to have done. Find the scale factor, then multiply. Lengths scale by k, areas by k squared, volumes by k cubed. Next time, trigonometry: sine, cosine and tangent. Good night, my dear friend.

I have retold it in my own words from the Wikipedia article Geometry, written by a great many hands and shared under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licence. The facts are theirs, checked as carefully as I am able; the jokes, I am afraid, are mine.
Tonight, a tour of geometry, from Egyptian rope-stretchers to the curved space of the twentieth century.
## Measuring the earth

The word geometry comes from the Greek for earth-measurement. The Greek historian Herodotus said that geometry began in Egypt, where the yearly flood of the Nile wiped out the boundaries of fields, and surveyors had to measure them out again. Whether or not that is the whole story, the Egyptians and Babylonians certainly knew practical rules for areas and volumes, and the Babylonians knew the relationship we call Pythagoras' theorem long before Pythagoras.
## Euclid

The Greeks turned these rules into a science of proof. Around three hundred years before Christ, Euclid of Alexandria wrote the Elements, thirteen books that begin with definitions, five postulates and some common notions, and derive from them hundreds of theorems about triangles, circles, parallels and solids. The Elements was used as a textbook for over two thousand years. I learned from it myself, by candlelight, and my cat is named in its author's honour, though he has never read it.
?? While I pour. What did Euclid start from, in building geometry?
=> A few definitions, postulates and common notions, taken as starting points, from which everything else was proved.
## Other Greek achievements

Archimedes found the areas and volumes of curved figures, such as the sphere. Apollonius studied the conic sections, the ellipse, parabola and hyperbola, made by slicing a cone. Eratosthenes measured the circumference of the Earth with a stick, a shadow and a good deal of thought. Later, Islamic and Indian mathematicians developed trigonometry, the measurement of triangles, for astronomy.
## Coordinates

In 1637 René Descartes, and independently Pierre de Fermat, joined geometry to algebra. Put a grid of coordinates on the plane, and every point becomes a pair of numbers, every line or curve an equation. Geometry could now be done by calculation. This analytic geometry made the calculus possible, and is the way we have been describing graphs in words on the ridge.
## Non-Euclidean geometry

Euclid's fifth postulate, about parallel lines, always seemed less obvious than the others. For two thousand years, mathematicians tried to prove it from the rest. In my own century, Lobachevsky, Bolyai and Gauss realised that it cannot be proved: one can build perfectly consistent geometries in which it is false. On the surface of a sphere, there are no parallels at all, and triangles have angles adding to more than one hundred and eighty degrees. In other geometries there are infinitely many parallels through a point. In 1854 Bernhard Riemann described geometry in curved spaces of any number of dimensions. Einstein later used Riemann's geometry in his theory of gravity, in which space itself is curved by matter.
## Topology and beyond

Topology, sometimes called rubber-sheet geometry, studies the properties of shapes that survive stretching and bending without tearing: a doughnut and a teacup, each with one hole, are the same to a topologist. Other modern branches include differential geometry, the study of curves and surfaces by calculus; projective geometry, the geometry of perspective; and the fractals of the twentieth century.
## Summary

Geometry, earth-measurement, grew from practical rules in Egypt and Babylon into Euclid's system of proof. Descartes joined it to algebra in 1637. Non-Euclidean geometry showed that Euclid's parallel postulate is not the only possibility, and Riemann's curved spaces led to Einstein. Topology studies shape without measurement.

I confess I have not yet found the time to retell this one in my own words, so the words are Wikipedia's, written by a great many hands, and I read them as faithfully as I can. I have adapted them only for listening: formulas are said in words, where a formula is displayed I add a short note in plain words, and now and then I interrupt with a remark of my own, which you will know by its frivolity.

Euclidean geometry is a mathematical system attributed to Euclid, an ancient Greek mathematician, which he described in his textbook on geometry, Elements. Euclid's approach consists in assuming a small set of intuitively appealing axioms (postulates) and deducing many other propositions (theorems) from these. One of those is the parallel postulate which relates to parallel lines on a Euclidean plane. Although many of Euclid's results had been stated earlier, Euclid was the first to organize these propositions into a logical system in which each result is proved from axioms and previously proved theorems.

The Elements begins with plane geometry, still taught in secondary school (high school) as the first axiomatic system and the first examples of mathematical proofs. It goes on to the solid geometry of three dimensions. Much of the Elements states results of what are now called algebra and number theory, explained in geometrical language.
For more than two thousand years, the adjective "Euclidean" was unnecessary because

Euclid's axioms seemed so intuitively obvious (with the possible exception of the parallel postulate) that theorems proved from them were deemed absolutely true, and thus no other sorts of geometry were possible. Today, however, two other self-consistent non-Euclidean geometries are known, hyperbolic and elliptic geometry. An implication of Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity is that physical space itself is not Euclidean, and Euclidean space is a good approximation for it only over short distances and weak gravity.

Euclidean geometry is an example of synthetic geometry, in that it proceeds logically from axioms describing basic properties of geometric objects such as points and lines, to propositions about those objects. This is in contrast to analytic geometry, introduced almost 2,000 years later by René Descartes, which uses coordinates to express geometric properties by means of algebraic formulas.

Classical geometry is sometimes used to refer to Euclid's methods of proof, by contrast with more recent methods, such as the use of coordinates (analytic geometry), the use of transformation groups (Erlangen program), or the use of calculus (differential geometry).
## The Elements

The Elements is mainly a systematization of earlier knowledge of geometry. Its improvement over earlier treatments was rapidly recognized, with the result that there was little interest in preserving the earlier ones, and they are now nearly all lost.
There are 13 books in the Elements:

Books I–IV and VI discuss plane geometry. Many results about plane figures are proved, for example, "In any triangle, two angles taken together in any manner are less than two right angles." (Book I proposition 17) and the Pythagorean theorem "In right-angled triangles the square on the side subtending the right angle is equal to the squares on the sides containing the right angle." (Book I, proposition 47)

Books V and VII–X deal with number theory, with numbers treated geometrically as lengths of line segments or areas of surface regions. Notions such as prime numbers and rational and irrational numbers are introduced. It is proved that there are infinitely many prime numbers.
Books XI–XIII concern solid geometry. A typical result is the 1:3 ratio between the volume of a cone and a cylinder with the same height and base. The platonic solids are constructed.
## Axioms

Euclidean geometry is an axiomatic system, in which all theorems ("true statements") are derived from a small number of simple axioms. Until the advent of non-Euclidean geometry, these axioms were considered to be obviously true in the physical world, so that all the theorems would be equally true. However, Euclid's reasoning from assumptions to conclusions remains valid independently from the physical reality.
Near the beginning of the first book of the Elements, Euclid gives five postulates (axioms) for plane geometry, stated in terms of constructions (as translated by Thomas Heath):
Let the following be postulated:
To draw a straight line from any point to any point.
To produce (extend) a finite straight line continuously in a straight line.
To describe a circle with any centre and distance (radius).
That all right angles are equal to one another.

[The parallel postulate]: That, if a straight line falling on two straight lines makes the interior angles on the same side less than two right angles, the two straight lines, if produced indefinitely, meet on that side on which the angles are less than two right angles.
Although Euclid explicitly only asserts the existence of the constructed objects, in his reasoning he also implicitly assumes them to be unique.
The Elements also include the following five "common notions":
Things that are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another (the transitive property of a Euclidean relation).
If equals are added to equals, then the wholes are equal (Addition property of equality).
If equals are subtracted from equals, then the differences are equal (subtraction property of equality).
Things that coincide with one another are equal to one another (reflexive property).
The whole is greater than the part.

Modern scholars agree that Euclid's postulates do not provide the complete logical foundation that Euclid required for his presentation. Modern treatments use more extensive and complete sets of axioms.
## Parallel postulate

To the ancients, the parallel postulate seemed less obvious than the others. They aspired to create a system of absolutely certain propositions, and to them, it seemed as if the parallel line postulate required proof from simpler statements. It is now known that such a proof is impossible since one can construct consistent systems of geometry (obeying the other axioms) in which the parallel postulate is true, and others in which it is false. Euclid himself seems to have considered it as being qualitatively different from the others, as evidenced by the organization of the Elements: his first 28 propositions are those that can be proved without it.
Many alternative axioms can be formulated which are logically equivalent to the parallel postulate (in the context of the other axioms). For example, Playfair's axiom states:
In a plane, through a point not on a given straight line, at most one line can be drawn that never meets the given line.
The "at most" clause is all that is needed since it can be proved from the remaining axioms that at least one parallel line exists.
## Methods of proof

Euclidean geometry is constructive. Postulates 1, 2, 3, and 5 assert the existence and uniqueness of certain geometric figures, and these assertions are of a constructive nature: that is, we are not only told that certain things exist, but are also given methods for creating them with no more than a compass and an unmarked straightedge. In this sense, Euclidean geometry is more concrete than many modern axiomatic systems such as set theory, which often assert the existence of objects without saying how to construct them, or even assert the existence of objects that cannot be constructed within the theory. Strictly speaking, the lines on paper are models of the objects defined within the formal system, rather than instances of those objects. For example, a Euclidean straight line has no width, but any real drawn line will have. Though nearly all modern mathematicians consider nonconstructive proofs just as sound as constructive ones, they are often considered less elegant, intuitive, or practically useful. Euclid's constructive proofs often supplanted fallacious nonconstructive ones, for example some Pythagorean proofs that assumed all numbers are rational, usually requiring a statement such as "Find the greatest common measure of..."
Euclid often used proof by contradiction.
## Naming of points and figures

Points are customarily named using capital letters of the alphabet. Other figures, such as lines, triangles, or circles, are named by listing a sufficient number of points to pick them out unambiguously from the relevant figure, for example triangle ABC would typically be a triangle with vertices at points A, B, and C.
## Complementary and supplementary angles

Angles whose sum is a right angle are called complementary. Complementary angles are formed when a ray shares the same vertex and is pointed in a direction that is in between the two original rays that form the right angle. The number of rays in between the two original rays is infinite.

Angles whose sum is a straight angle are supplementary. Supplementary angles are formed when a ray shares the same vertex and is pointed in a direction that is in between the two original rays that form the straight angle (180 degree angle). The number of rays in between the two original rays is infinite.
## Modern versions of Euclid's notation
In modern terminology, angles would normally be measured in degrees or radians.

Modern school textbooks often define separate figures called lines (infinite), rays (semi-infinite), and line segments (of finite length). Euclid, rather than discussing a ray as an object that extends to infinity in one direction, would normally use locutions such as "if the line is extended to a sufficient length", although he occasionally referred to "infinite lines". A "line" for Euclid could be either straight or curved, and he used the more specific term "straight line" when necessary.
## Pons asinorum

The pons asinorum (bridge of asses) states that in isosceles triangles the angles at the base equal one another, and, if the equal straight lines are produced further, then the angles under the base equal one another. Its name may be attributed to its frequent role as the first real test in the Elements of the intelligence of the reader and as a bridge to the harder propositions that followed. It might also be so named because of the geometrical figure's resemblance to a steep bridge that only a sure-footed donkey could cross.

## Congruence of triangles
Triangles are congruent if they satisfy any of the following (Book I, propositions 4, 8, and 26):
SSS — all three sides equal; SAS — two sides and the included angle equal; ASA — two angles and the included side equal.
Triangles with three equal angles (AAA) are similar, but not necessarily congruent. Likewise, two equal sides and a non-included angle (SSA) do not guarantee congruence.
## Triangle angle sum
The sum of the angles of a triangle is equal to a straight angle:
This means an equilateral triangle has three 60 degrees interior angles, and every triangle has at least two acute angles and at most one obtuse or right angle.
## Pythagorean theorem
The celebrated Pythagorean theorem (Book I, proposition 47) states that in any right triangle with legs a, b and hypotenuse c:
The area of the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the areas of the squares on the two legs.
## Thales' theorem
Thales' theorem, named after Thales of Miletus, states that if A, B, and C lie on a circle with AC as a diameter, then:
Cantor supposed that Thales proved this by means of Euclid Book I, Prop. 32, following the manner of Euclid Book III, Prop. 31.
## Ptolemy's theorem
Ptolemy's theorem relates the sides and diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral (a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle). For a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD:
⟦A C ⋅ B D = A B ⋅ C D + B C ⋅ D A⟧

That is, the product of the diagonals equals the sum of the products of opposite sides. The theorem generalizes the Pythagorean theorem, recovered as the special case where the cyclic quadrilateral is a rectangle. Ptolemy, in the Almagest, used the result to construct his table of chords, a precursor to modern trigonometric tables.
## The five Platonic solids

Book XIII of the Elements, its final book, is devoted to the construction and classification of the Platonic solids — the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron — each a convex polyhedron whose faces are congruent regular polygons meeting in the same arrangement at every vertex. Propositions 13–17 construct these five solids in turn, and for each Euclid finds the ratio of the diameter of the circumscribed sphere to the edge length. Proposition 18 argues that no further convex regular polyhedron exists.
## Scaling of area and volume
In modern terminology, the area of a plane figure is proportional to the square of any of its linear dimensions, and the volume of a solid to the cube:

Euclid proved these results in various special cases such as the area of a circle and the volume of a parallelepipedal solid. Euclid determined some, but not all, of the relevant constants of proportionality. For instance, it was his successor Archimedes who proved that a sphere has 2/3 the volume of the circumscribing cylinder.
## System of measurement and arithmetic

Euclidean geometry has two fundamental types of measurements: angle and distance. The angle scale is absolute, and Euclid uses the right angle as his basic unit, so that, for example, a 45-degree angle would be referred to as half of a right angle. The distance scale is relative; one arbitrarily picks a line segment with a certain nonzero length as the unit, and other distances are expressed in relation to it. Addition of distances is represented by a construction in which one line segment is copied onto the end of another line segment to extend its length, and similarly for subtraction.

Measurements of area and volume are derived from distances. For example, a rectangle with a width of 3 and a length of 4 has an area that represents the product, 12. Because this geometrical interpretation of multiplication was limited to three dimensions, there was no direct way of interpreting the product of four or more numbers, and Euclid avoided such products, although they are implied, for example in the proof of book IX, proposition 20.

Euclid refers to a pair of lines, or a pair of planar or solid figures, as "equal" if their lengths, areas, or volumes are equal respectively, and similarly for angles. The stronger term "congruent" refers to the idea that an entire figure is the same size and shape as another figure. Alternatively, two figures are congruent if one can be moved on top of the other so that it matches up with it exactly. (Flipping it over is allowed.) Thus, for example, a 2x6 rectangle and a 3x4 rectangle are equal but not congruent, and the letter R is congruent to its mirror image. Figures that would be congruent except for their differing sizes are referred to as similar. Corresponding angles in a pair of similar shapes are equal and corresponding sides are in proportion to each other.

Stress analysis: Stress analysis - Euclidean geometry is pivotal in determining stress distribution in mechanical components, which is essential for ensuring structural integrity and durability.

Gear design: Gear - The design of gears, a crucial element in many mechanical systems, relies heavily on Euclidean geometry to ensure proper tooth shape and engagement for efficient power transmission.

Heat exchanger design: Heat exchanger - In thermal engineering, Euclidean geometry is used to design heat exchangers, where the geometric configuration greatly influences thermal efficiency. See shell-and-tube heat exchangers and plate heat exchangers for more details.

Lens design: Lens - In optical engineering, Euclidean geometry is critical in the design of lenses, where precise geometric shapes determine the focusing properties. Geometric optics analyzes the focusing of light by lenses and mirrors.

Computer Aided Design (CAD) and Manufacturing (CAM): Translates physical shapes into Cartesian coordinates (x, y, z), using special transformations like translation, scaling, and reflection to model machine parts.
## Dynamics

Vibration analysis: Vibration - Euclidean geometry is essential in analyzing and understanding the vibrations in mechanical systems, aiding in the design of systems that can withstand or utilize these vibrations effectively.

Wing design: Aircraft Wing Design - The application of Euclidean geometry in aerodynamics is evident in aircraft wing design, airfoils, and hydrofoils where geometric shape directly impacts lift and drag characteristics.

Satellite orbits: Satellite Orbits - Euclidean geometry helps in calculating and predicting the orbits of satellites, essential for successful space missions and satellite operations. Also see astrodynamics, celestial mechanics, and elliptic orbit.
## CAD systems

3D modeling: In CAD (computer-aided design) systems, Euclidean geometry is fundamental for creating accurate 3D models of mechanical parts. These models are crucial for visualizing and testing designs before manufacturing.

Design and manufacturing: Much of CAM (computer-aided manufacturing) relies on Euclidean geometry. The design geometry in CAD/CAM typically consists of shapes bounded by planes, cylinders, cones, tori, and other similar Euclidean forms. Today, CAD/CAM is essential in the design of a wide range of products, from cars and airplanes to ships and smartphones.

Evolution of drafting practices: Historically, advanced Euclidean geometry, including theorems like Pascal's theorem and Brianchon's theorem, was integral to drafting practices. However, with the advent of modern CAD systems, such in-depth knowledge of these theorems is less necessary in contemporary design and manufacturing processes.

PCB layouts: Printed circuit board (PCB) design utilizes Euclidean geometry for the efficient placement and routing of components, ensuring functionality while optimizing space. Efficient layout of electronic components on PCBs is critical for minimizing signal interference and optimizing circuit performance.

Antenna design: Antenna design - Euclidean geometry of antennas helps in designing antennas, where the spatial arrangement and dimensions directly affect antenna and array performance in transmitting and receiving electromagnetic waves.

Field theory: Complex potential flow - In the study of inviscid flow fields and electromagnetic fields, Euclidean geometry aids in visualizing and solving potential flow problems. This is essential for understanding fluid velocity field and electromagnetic field interactions in three-dimensional space. The relationship of which is characterized by an irrotational solenoidal field or a conservative vector field.
## Controls

Control system analysis: Control systems - The application of Euclidean geometry in control theory helps in the analysis and design of control systems, particularly in understanding and optimizing system stability and response.

Calculation tools: Jacobian - Euclidean geometry is integral in using Jacobian matrices for transformations and control systems in both mechanical and electrical engineering fields, providing insights into system behavior and properties. The Jacobian serves as a linearized design matrix in statistical regression and curve fitting; see non-linear least squares. The Jacobian is also used in random matrices, moment, statistics, and diagnostics.
## Other general applications
Because of Euclidean geometry's fundamental status in mathematics, it is impractical to give more than a representative sampling of applications here.

As suggested by the etymology of the word, one of the earliest reasons for interest in and also one of the most common current uses of geometry is surveying. In addition it has been used in classical mechanics and the cognitive and computational approaches to visual perception of objects. Certain practical results from Euclidean geometry (such as the right-angle property of the 3-4-5 triangle) were used long before they were proved formally. The fundamental types of measurements in Euclidean geometry are distances and angles, both of which can be measured directly by a surveyor. Historically, distances were often measured by chains, such as Gunter's chain, and angles using graduated circles and, later, the theodolite.

An application of Euclidean solid geometry is the determination of packing arrangements, such as the problem of finding the most efficient packing of spheres in n dimensions. This problem has applications in error detection and correction.
Geometry is used extensively in architecture.
Geometry can be used to design origami. Some classical construction problems of geometry are impossible using compass and straightedge, but can be solved using origami.

## Archimedes and Apollonius

Archimedes (around 287 BC – around 212 BC), a colorful figure about whom many historical anecdotes are recorded, is remembered along with Euclid as one of the greatest of ancient mathematicians. Although the foundations of his work were put in place by Euclid, his work, unlike Euclid's, is believed to have been entirely original. He proved equations for the volumes and areas of various figures in two and three dimensions, and enunciated the Archimedean property of finite numbers.
Apollonius of Perga (around 240 BC – around 190 BC) is mainly known for his investigation of conic sections.
## 17th century: Descartes
René Descartes (1596–1650) developed analytic geometry, an alternative method for formalizing geometry which focused on turning geometry into algebra.
In this approach, a point on a plane is represented by its Cartesian (x, y) coordinates, a line is represented by its equation, and so on.

In Euclid's original approach, the Pythagorean theorem follows from Euclid's axioms. In the Cartesian approach, the axioms are the axioms of algebra, and the equation expressing the Pythagorean theorem is then a definition of one of the terms in Euclid's axioms, which are now considered theorems.
The equation
A formula is omitted here.

Also in the 17th century, Girard Desargues, motivated by the theory of perspective, introduced the concept of idealized points, lines, and planes at infinity. The result can be considered as a type of generalized geometry, projective geometry, but it can also be used to produce proofs in ordinary Euclidean geometry in which the number of special cases is reduced.
## 18th century

Geometers of the 18th century struggled to define the boundaries of the Euclidean system. Many tried in vain to prove the fifth postulate from the first four. By 1763, at least 28 different proofs had been published, but all were found incorrect.

Leading up to this period, geometers also tried to determine what constructions could be accomplished in Euclidean geometry. For example, the problem of trisecting an angle with a compass and straightedge is one that naturally occurs within the theory, since the axioms refer to constructive operations that can be carried out with those tools. However, centuries of efforts failed to find a solution to this problem, until Pierre Wantzel published a proof in 1837 that such a construction was impossible. Other constructions that were proved impossible include doubling the cube and squaring the circle. In the case of doubling the cube, the impossibility of the construction originates from the fact that the compass and straightedge method involve equations whose order is an integral power of two, while doubling a cube requires the solution of a third-order equation.

Euler discussed a generalization of Euclidean geometry called affine geometry, which retains the fifth postulate unmodified while weakening postulates three and four in a way that eliminates the notions of angle (whence right triangles become meaningless) and of equality of length of line segments in general (whence circles become meaningless) while retaining the notions of parallelism as an equivalence relation between lines, and equality of length of parallel line segments (so line segments continue to have a midpoint).
## 19th century
In the early 19th century, Carnot and Möbius systematically developed the use of signed angles and line segments as a way of simplifying and unifying results.
## Higher dimensions

In the 1840s William Rowan Hamilton developed the quaternions, and John T. Graves and Arthur Cayley the octonions. These are normed algebras which extend the complex numbers. Later it was understood that the quaternions are also a Euclidean geometric system with four real Cartesian coordinates. Cayley used quaternions to study rotations in 4-dimensional Euclidean space.

At mid-century Ludwig Schläfli developed the general concept of Euclidean space, extending Euclidean geometry to higher dimensions. He defined polyschemes, later called polytopes, which are the higher-dimensional analogues of polygons and polyhedra. He developed their theory and discovered all the regular polytopes, that is the ⟦n⟧-dimensional analogues of regular polygons and Platonic solids. He found there are six regular convex polytopes in dimension four, and three in all higher dimensions.

Schläfli performed this work in relative obscurity and it was published in full only posthumously in 1901. It had little influence until it was rediscovered and fully documented in 1948 by H. S. M. Coxeter.

In 1878 William Kingdon Clifford introduced what is now termed geometric algebra, unifying Hamilton's quaternions with Hermann Grassmann's algebra and revealing the geometric nature of these systems, especially in four dimensions. The operations of the Clifford algebra have the effect of mirroring, rotating, translating, and mapping the geometric objects that are being modeled to new positions. The Clifford torus on the surface of the 3-sphere is the simplest and most symmetric flat embedding of the Cartesian product of two circles (in the same sense that the surface of a cylinder is "flat").
## Non-Euclidean geometry

The century's most influential development in geometry occurred when, around 1830, János Bolyai and Nikolai Ivanovich Lobachevsky separately published work on non-Euclidean geometry, in which the parallel postulate is not valid. Since non-Euclidean geometry is provably relatively consistent with Euclidean geometry, the parallel postulate cannot be proved from the other postulates.

In the 19th century, it was also realized that Euclid's ten axioms and common notions do not suffice to prove all of the theorems stated in the Elements. For example, Euclid assumed implicitly that any line contains at least two points, but this assumption cannot be proved from the other axioms, and therefore must be an axiom itself. The very first geometric proof in the Elements, shown in the figure above, is that any line segment is part of a triangle; Euclid constructs this in the usual way, by drawing circles around both endpoints and taking their intersection as the third vertex. His axioms, however, do not guarantee that the circles actually intersect, because they do not assert the geometrical property of continuity, which in Cartesian terms is equivalent to the completeness property of the real numbers. Starting with Moritz Pasch in 1882, many improved axiomatic systems for geometry have been proposed, the best known being those of Hilbert, George Birkhoff, and Tarski.
## 20th century and relativity

Einstein's theory of special relativity involves a four-dimensional space-time, the Minkowski space, which is non-Euclidean. This shows that non-Euclidean geometries, which had been introduced a few years earlier for showing that the parallel postulate cannot be proved, are also useful for describing the physical world.

However, the three-dimensional "space part" of the Minkowski space remains the space of Euclidean geometry. This is not the case with general relativity, for which the geometry of the space part of space-time is not Euclidean geometry. For example, if a triangle is constructed out of three rays of light, then in general the interior angles do not add up to 180 degrees due to gravity. A relatively weak gravitational field, such as the Earth's or the Sun's, is represented by a metric that is approximately, but not exactly, Euclidean. Until the 20th century, there was no technology capable of detecting these deviations in rays of light from Euclidean geometry, but Einstein predicted that such deviations would exist. They were later verified by observations such as the slight bending of starlight by the Sun during a solar eclipse in 1919, and such considerations are now an integral part of the software that runs the GPS system.
## As a description of the structure of space

Euclid believed that his axioms were self-evident statements about physical reality. Euclid's proofs depend upon assumptions perhaps not obvious in Euclid's fundamental axioms, in particular that certain movements of figures do not change their geometrical properties such as the lengths of sides and interior angles, the so-called Euclidean motions, which include translations, reflections and rotations of figures. Taken as a physical description of space, postulate 2 (extending a line) asserts that space does not have holes or boundaries; postulate 4 (equality of right angles) says that space is isotropic and figures may be moved to any location while maintaining congruence; and postulate 5 (the parallel postulate) that space is flat (has no intrinsic curvature).
As discussed above, Albert Einstein's theory of relativity significantly modifies this view.

The ambiguous character of the axioms as originally formulated by Euclid makes it possible for different commentators to disagree about some of their other implications for the structure of space, such as whether or not it is infinite (see below) and what its topology is. Modern, more rigorous reformulations of the system typically aim for a cleaner separation of these issues. Interpreting Euclid's axioms in the spirit of this more modern approach, axioms 1–4 are consistent with either infinite or finite space (as in elliptic geometry), and all five axioms are consistent with a variety of topologies (for example a plane, a cylinder, or a torus for two-dimensional Euclidean geometry).

## Infinite objects

Euclid sometimes distinguished explicitly between "finite lines" (for example Postulate 2) and "infinite lines" (book I, proposition 12). However, he typically did not make such distinctions unless they were necessary. The postulates do not explicitly refer to infinite lines, although for example some commentators interpret postulate 3, existence of a circle with any radius, as implying that space is infinite.

The notion of infinitesimal quantities had previously been discussed extensively by the Eleatic School, but nobody had been able to put them on a firm logical basis, with paradoxes such as Zeno's paradox occurring that had not been resolved to universal satisfaction. Euclid used the method of exhaustion rather than infinitesimals.

Later ancient commentators, such as Proclus (410–485 AD), treated many questions about infinity as issues demanding proof and, for example Proclus claimed to prove the infinite divisibility of a line, based on a proof by contradiction in which he considered the cases of even and odd numbers of points constituting it.

At the turn of the 20th century, Otto Stolz, Paul du Bois-Reymond, Giuseppe Veronese, and others produced controversial work on non-Archimedean models of Euclidean geometry, in which the distance between two points may be infinite or infinitesimal, in the Newton–Leibniz sense. Fifty years later, Abraham Robinson provided a rigorous logical foundation for Veronese's work.
## Infinite processes

Ancient geometers may have considered the parallel postulate – that two parallel lines do not ever intersect – less certain than the others because it makes a statement about infinitely remote regions of space, and so cannot be physically verified.

The modern formulation of proof by induction was not developed until the 17th century, but some later commentators consider it implicit in some of Euclid's proofs, for example the proof of the infinitude of primes.

Supposed paradoxes involving infinite series, such as Zeno's paradox, predated Euclid. Euclid avoided such discussions, giving, for example, the expression for the partial sums of the geometric series in IX.35 without commenting on the possibility of letting the number of terms become infinite.

In mathematics, the Pythagorean theorem or Pythagoras's theorem is a fundamental relation in Euclidean geometry between the three sides of a right triangle. It states that the area of the square whose side is the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle) is equal to the sum of the areas of the squares on the other two sides.
The theorem can be written as an equation relating the lengths of the sides ⟦a⟧, ⟦b⟧ and the hypotenuse ⟦c⟧, sometimes called the Pythagorean equation:
In plain words: it says that the two sides are equal. A power means multiplying a number by itself a given number of times.

The theorem is named for the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, born around 570 BC. The theorem has been proved numerous times by many different methods – possibly the most for any mathematical theorem. The proofs are diverse, including both geometric proofs and algebraic proofs, with some dating back thousands of years.

When Euclidean space is represented by a Cartesian coordinate system in analytic geometry, Euclidean distance satisfies the Pythagorean relation: the squared distance between two points equals the sum of squares of the difference in each coordinate between the points.

The theorem can be generalized in various ways: to higher-dimensional spaces, to spaces that are not Euclidean, to objects that are not right triangles, and to objects that are not triangles at all but ⟦n⟧-dimensional solids.
## History

Forms of the Pythagorean theorem have appeared in many ancient cultures, and the date of first discovery is uncertain, as is the date of the first proof. The history of the development of the theorem involves multiple aspects, including calculations regarding specific right triangles, knowledge of Pythagorean triples, understanding the relationship among the sides of a right triangle, and proofs of the theorem within some deductive system.

Written around 1800 BC, the Egyptian Middle Kingdom Berlin Papyrus 6619 includes a problem involving two squares whose areas sum to a third square, whose solution is the Pythagorean triple 6:8:10, but the problem does not mention a triangle. According to Plutarch, writing many centuries later, the ancient Egyptians did know about the 3:4:5 right triangle, identifying its sides with Osiris, Isis, and Horus respectively.

Historians of Mesopotamian mathematics have concluded that the Pythagorean rule was in widespread use during the Old Babylonian period (20th to 16th centuries BC), over a thousand years before Pythagoras was born. The Mesopotamian tablet Plimpton 322, written near Larsa also around 1800 BC, contains entries that can be interpreted as the sides and diagonals of 15 different Pythagorean triples. Another tablet from a similar time, YBC 7289, calculates the diagonal of a square or, equivalently, of an isosceles right triangle.

In India, the Baudhayana Shulba Sutra, the dates of which are given variously as between the 8th and 5th century BC, contains a list of Pythagorean triples and a statement of the Pythagorean theorem, both in the special case of the isosceles right triangle and in the general case, as does the Apastamba Shulba Sutra (around 600 BC).

Byzantine Neoplatonic philosopher and mathematician Proclus, writing in the fifth century AD, states two arithmetic rules, "one of them attributed to Plato, the other to Pythagoras", for generating special Pythagorean triples. The rule attributed to Pythagoras (around 570 – around 495 BC) starts from an odd number and produces a triple with leg and hypotenuse differing by one unit; the rule attributed to Plato (428/427 or 424/423 – 348/347 BC) starts from an even number and produces a triple with leg and hypotenuse differing by two units. According to Thomas L. Heath (1861–1940), no specific attribution of the theorem to Pythagoras exists in the surviving Greek literature from the five centuries after Pythagoras lived. However, when authors such as Plutarch and Cicero attributed the theorem to Pythagoras, they did so in a way which suggests that the attribution was widely known and undoubted. Classicist Kurt von Fritz wrote, "Whether this formula is rightly attributed to Pythagoras personally... one can safely assume that it belongs to the very oldest period of Pythagorean mathematics." Around 300 BC, in Euclid's Elements, the oldest extant axiomatic proof of the theorem is presented, along with Euclid's formula for generating all primitive Pythagorean triples.

With contents known much earlier, but in surviving texts dating from roughly the 1st century BC, the Chinese text Zhoubi Suanjing, (The Arithmetical Classic of the Gnomon and the Circular Paths of Heaven) gives a reasoning for the Pythagorean theorem for the (3, 4, 5) triangle — in China it is called the "Gougu theorem". During the Han Dynasty (202 BC to 220 AD), Pythagorean triples appear in The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art, together with a mention of right triangles. Some believe the theorem arose first in China in the 11th century BC, where it is alternatively known as the "Shang Gao theorem", named after the Duke of Zhou's astronomer and mathematician, whose reasoning composed most of what was in the Zhoubi Suanjing.

English mathematician Sir Thomas Heath gives this proof in his commentary on Proposition I.47 in Euclid's Elements, and mentions the proposals of German mathematicians Carl Anton Bretschneider and Hermann Hankel that Pythagoras may have known this proof. Heath himself favors a different proposal for a Pythagorean proof, but acknowledges from the outset of his discussion "that the Greek literature which we possess belonging to the first five centuries after Pythagoras contains no statement specifying this or any other particular great geometric discovery to him." Recent scholarship has cast increasing doubt on any sort of role for Pythagoras as a creator of mathematics, although debate about this continues.
