Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight I begin a story from my own era: Flatland, a romance of many dimensions, by Edwin Abbott Abbott, headmaster of the City of London School, published in 1884 under the pen name A Square. The book is in the public domain, and I have retold its first part, This World, in my own words, in 3 lectures. This is the first.
## A book from my own era

Let me tell you about a book that appeared in London when I was a man of fifty-five, and which I read with great delight. It is called Flatland: A Romance of Many Dimensions. Its author signed himself A Square, but he was in fact the Reverend Edwin Abbott Abbott, a clergyman and scholar, headmaster of the City of London School, and a great believer in the education of everybody, girls included. Keep that last fact in mind, my friend, for the narrator of the book holds some opinions which Abbott was holding up to ridicule.

The story is told by a Square, a respectable professional gentleman of a world with only two dimensions. In the first part of the book, which I shall retell over three evenings, he describes his world and its customs. In the second part, which we shall not reach, he travels to worlds of one and three dimensions, and his life is turned upside down.
## A world like a sheet of paper

Imagine, says the Square, a vast sheet of paper, on which straight lines, triangles, squares, pentagons, hexagons and other figures move freely about, on or in the surface, but without the power of rising above it or sinking below it. Rather like shadows, only hard and with luminous edges. That is Flatland. Its people have length and breadth, but no height at all.

Now here is the first great point. Take a penny and lay it flat on a table. Look down on it from above, and it is a circle. Now bring your eye down to the very edge of the table, and look along the surface. The penny becomes, as you lower your eye, an oval, then a thinner oval, and at last, when your eye is exactly at the level of the table top, a straight line. That is how a Flatlander sees everything. He cannot look down from above, because there is no above. A triangle, a square, a circle: all look to him like straight lines, brighter in some parts and dimmer in others.
?? While I pour. If everyone in Flatland looks like a line, how might they tell a triangle from a square?
=> By the way the line fades into the distance at its ends, by feeling, and by voice. The Square explains all three, as you shall hear.
## Weather and houses

Flatland has no sun as we have it, and no windows, for its light, the Square says, comes from everywhere equally, whence nobody knows. Its learned men so wore themselves out over the origin of light that the government at last forbade the question altogether. The Square adds, with feeling, that he alone now knows the answer, and is thought a madman for it. That is a hint of what is coming in the second half of the book.

There is, however, a steady rain, which always falls from the north, and that gives Flatlanders their compass. Houses are built to keep it off. The commonest house is a pentagon, five-sided, with its roof, the two sides facing north, pointing into the rain. There is a large door on the west for men, and a small one on the east for women. Square and triangular houses are forbidden, because their sharp corners are dangerous to passers-by, who cannot see them clearly, being themselves only able to see lines.
## The ranks of society
Here is the satire. In Flatland, a person's rank depends on his shape.

Women are straight lines. Soldiers and the lowest workmen are isosceles triangles, that is, triangles with two long equal sides of about eleven inches and a very short base, perhaps half an inch, so that they come to a very sharp point. The middle class are equilateral triangles, with three equal sides. Professional men and gentlemen, like our narrator, are squares and pentagons. Above them come the nobility, hexagons and figures of more and more sides. And when a figure has so many tiny sides that it cannot be told from a circle, he joins the highest order of all: the Circles, who are the priests, and rule the country.

The more sides, the higher the rank, and the cleverer, so the Flatlanders believe, for to them a larger angle means a larger mind. An isosceles soldier with his needle-sharp point is thought to be little better than a weapon.
## The law of nature

And there is a law of nature in Flatland. The son of a regular figure has one more side than his father. The son of a square is a pentagon; the son of a pentagon, a hexagon; and so up the ladder, generation by generation. So the Square is the father of pentagons and the grandfather of hexagons, which pleases him enormously.
?? While I take a sip. By this law, how many generations after a square would a family first produce a figure with ten sides?
=> Six. The square has four sides; five, six, seven, eight, nine and ten sides take six more generations.

But the rule does not hold for the irregular classes. The son of an isosceles is still an isosceles. Only after long generations of good conduct, careful marriages arranged by the priests, and frugality, does an isosceles family occasionally produce a true equilateral triangle. When it happens, the whole neighbourhood rejoices, and the child is taken from its parents and brought up by a childless equilateral family, so that it shall never be dragged back down by its relations. The Square relates this with entire approval. Abbott, you may be sure, did not.
## What Abbott was doing

You will have noticed, my dear friend, that Flatland is a mirror held up to Victorian England. The soldiers and labourers at the bottom, the professional men in the middle, the aristocracy above, and the clergy at the top. A belief that birth and shape decide a person's worth. And a system that lets a very few of the lower classes rise, provided they are taken away from their families. Abbott, a headmaster who had risen by scholarship and believed in education for all, was laughing at all of it, through the mouth of a narrator who takes it perfectly seriously.

And he was teaching geometry at the same time. To imagine a world of two dimensions, and the way its people would see, is the first step towards imagining what it would be like if there were more than three. That is where the book is going. But not tonight.
## Summary

Flatland, published in 1884 by Edwin Abbott Abbott under the name A Square, is a world of two dimensions. Its inhabitants see each other edge-on, as lines. Rain falls from the north, and houses are pentagons. Rank depends on the number of sides: women are lines, soldiers sharp isosceles triangles, gentlemen squares and pentagons, nobles polygons, and the priests circles. The son of a regular figure has one more side than his father. And the whole is a satire on the class system of my own England.
That is the end of lecture 1 of my retelling of Flatland. Lecture 2 follows.
Flatland, retold, continued. This is lecture 2 of 3.
## Where we were

Last time, the Square told us about his flat world: its rain from the north, its pentagonal houses, and its people, whose rank depends on the number of their sides. Tonight he speaks about the women of Flatland, about how anyone recognises anyone else in a world where everyone looks like a line, and about the fate of those who are irregular. Some of it is uncomfortable, and is meant to be.
## The women of Flatland

The women of Flatland are straight lines. Seen from the side, a woman is a line, but seen end-on she is a mere point, almost invisible. And her end is sharp. If a soldier is a wedge, says the Square, a woman is a needle. A careless gentleman walking into a lady end-on might be pierced through and killed.

So the men of Flatland have hemmed the women in with laws. Every woman in a public place must keep up a continual cry, the peace-cry, so that people know she is near. She must keep moving her back gently from side to side, so that she is never invisible. Women must use the separate door on the east side of every house. And they are kept, the Square explains, entirely without education, for their minds, he assures us, are as narrow as their bodies.

Now, my dear friend, I must step out of the story for a moment, as Abbott wanted his readers to. The Square says all this as though it were perfectly natural, and adds that women have little memory, and are easily roused to fury. Abbott, in real life, was a champion of education for girls and women. In a preface to a later edition, he has the Square's editor remark that the Square's views on women had been changing. The cruelty and absurdity of Flatland's treatment of women is the target of the satire, not its message. Abbott was showing his Victorian readers their own prejudices, flattened out so that they could see them plainly.
?? While I pour. Why would a woman be most dangerous to a man walking directly towards one of her ends?
=> Because end-on she looks like a single point, nearly invisible, and her end is as sharp as a needle.
## How to recognise a friend
In a world where every figure looks like a line, how do you know whether you are speaking to a tradesman or a duke? The Square describes three methods.
The first is hearing. Every class has its own kind of voice, and a well-trained ear can tell them apart. But voices can be imitated, and so the method is not trusted entirely.

The second is feeling. Among women and the lower classes, recognition is done by touch. One person says to another, let me introduce my friend, and they gently feel each other's angles. A practised feeler can tell a square from a pentagon by a single touch of a corner. It is a little like shaking hands, done more thoroughly. Among the upper classes, feeling is thought vulgar, and a gentleman would rather not be felt at all.

The third method, the one prized by the upper classes, is sight, and it depends on fog. Fog fills Flatland most of the year. In fog, things farther away look dimmer. So when you look at a figure, the part nearest to you is bright, and the parts that slope away from you fade. A triangle with its point towards you shows a bright middle fading rapidly towards each end. A pentagon, whose sides slope away less steeply, fades more gently. By judging how quickly a line fades towards its ends, an educated Flatlander can tell the angle at its nearest corner, and so its shape. This art of sight recognition is taught for years at the universities, and the upper classes are very proud of it.
?? Which would fade more slowly towards its ends: a figure with a sharp angle facing you, or one with a wide angle?
=> The figure with the wide angle. Its sides slope away from you more gently, so they stay nearer, and brighter, for longer.

Notice, my friend, that the Square is teaching real geometry here, and real optics. He is describing how a two-dimensional being could judge depth from brightness, rather as we judge distance in a misty landscape.
## The irregulars

Now the darkest part of the first half. In Flatland, a figure whose sides or angles are not equal is called irregular. Since rank is shape, and recognition depends on regular angles, an irregular figure is a kind of fraud: you cannot tell what he is. So, says the Square, irregulars are watched from birth. A child found to be irregular by the official examination is, in the milder cases, straightened by force in hospital, and in the worse cases, destroyed. Irregular grown-ups are kept out of public life, and the law presumes them to be criminals.

The Square approves of this too, though he admits, a little uneasily, that some irregulars have been kind and clever. Abbott's readers would have recognised the habit of treating people as wicked because of how they were born, and the confident cruelty of respectable people who call it order.
## The ancient practice of painting

Before we part, the Square begins to tell an old story. In ancient times, he says, there lived a pentagon named Chromatistes, who discovered how to make paint, and began to colour himself and his house. Soon everyone wanted to be coloured. With colour, recognition became easy and delightful: a person's sides could be painted in different shades, and anyone could see his shape at a glance, without years of study and without feeling. The arts of sight recognition and of feeling fell out of use. Flatland, for a time, became beautiful. But the priests, the Circles, were not pleased. What happened next, I shall tell you tomorrow evening.
## Summary

In Flatland, women are straight lines, sharp as needles, governed by harsh laws; the Square approves, and Abbott, a champion of women's education, is mocking him. Flatlanders recognise each other by voice, by feeling the angles, and by sight in fog, judging an angle from how quickly a line fades. Irregular figures are treated with great cruelty. And long ago, the painter Chromatistes brought colour into Flatland.
That is the end of lecture 2 of my retelling of Flatland. Lecture 3 follows.
Flatland, retold, continued. This is lecture 3 of 3.
## Where we were

Last time, the Square told us how the pentagon Chromatistes brought paint into Flatland, and how colour spread, so that everyone could read anyone's shape at a glance. Tonight, the end of the story, and the end of the first part of the book.
## The Universal Colour Bill

With colour everywhere, the old arts of recognition by sight and by feeling began to die out. Why spend years at a university learning to read angles in the fog, when a glance at a painted side would do? And here, says the Square, was the danger. If everyone could look anything they pleased, the lower classes could pass for higher ones. An isosceles soldier, painted cleverly, might be taken for an equilateral, or worse.

The colour party, now very strong, proposed a Universal Colour Bill, to make colour compulsory for all, the priests included. The Circles had so far kept themselves uncoloured. The Square explains, with a diagram, that a priest painted half red and half green, seen from a certain angle, would look exactly like a young woman painted the same way. A priest might be mistaken for a lady. To the Square, this is the end of civilisation. The women, he notes darkly, were rather in favour.
?? While I pour. Why did colour threaten the power of the upper classes?
=> Because rank was read from shape, and colour let people of any shape be recognised and seem alike, so that rank could no longer be read so easily, or could be disguised.
## The trick of Pantocyclus

The crisis came at a great assembly. The chief Circle of the day, whose name was Pantocyclus, rose to speak before a hundred and twenty thousand angry isosceles soldiers, and astonished them by announcing that the Circles would give way, and accept the Colour Bill. Uproar turned to applause. He invited Chromatistes, the leader of the revolt, into the centre of the hall.

Then Pantocyclus made a speech, which the Square says lasted nearly a day. He turned group by group to the audience, and frightened each in turn. To the workmen he said: under colour, your hopes of rising, of having children with more sides, will vanish, because no one will be able to tell regular from irregular. To the women he cried that no marriage would be safe, and he ended: sooner than this, come death.

Those words were a signal. Convicts, placed by the Circles, fell upon Chromatistes and killed him. Lines of women, directed by the priests, moved back foremost, invisibly, upon the soldiers. The soldiers, attacked by enemies they could not see, cried treachery, and turned their sharp points on one another. Within half an hour, the Square reports, not one of that vast multitude was living. In the purge that followed, many more irregulars were destroyed, and colour was abolished by law, and soon all but forgotten. Flatland went back to grey.

The Square calls this the triumph of order. Abbott calls it nothing, and lets the reader judge. I need hardly tell you, my dear friend, which is the right judgement. A ruling class, threatened by something that made people equal, saved itself by a speech full of fear, and by turning the poor against each other.
## The rule of the Circles

The Square then describes the priests who rule Flatland. The Circles control every department: government, the law, the universities, the arts. Their teaching is summed up in one maxim: attend to your configuration. In other words, everything about you, your character, your virtue, your crimes, is a matter of your shape. If a man is wicked, it is because his angles are wrong, and the cure is to be found in the hospital, not in a sermon. If a child behaves badly, it is said, he has a bad angle.

And so, in Flatland, no one is responsible for anything, and no one may complain of anything, since all is shape, and shape is fixed by birth. The Square presents this philosophy with pride, and I think Abbott meant us to notice that it is the perfect creed for those already at the top.
?? While I take a sip of tea. Why is attend to your configuration a convenient teaching for those at the top of Flatland's society?
=> Because it says that everyone's worth is fixed by their shape, which is fixed by birth, so the existing order is natural, and cannot be questioned.
## The end of part one

The first part of Flatland, This World, ends here. The Square has described his home: its geometry, its laws, its cruelties, and his own comfortable place in it. In the second part, Other Worlds, he dreams of Lineland, a world of one dimension, whose king cannot imagine the Square's world. Then he is visited by a Sphere from Spaceland, our own three-dimensional world, which he cannot at first imagine any more than the King of Lineland could imagine him. He is lifted out of his plane, sees his whole country from above, and returns home with the truth about dimensions. And, having dared to speak of a third dimension, he is put in prison by the Circles.

So the book that began as a satire ends as a lesson in humility of the imagination. If a square cannot picture a sphere, perhaps we, in three dimensions, should not be too sure that there is nothing beyond. Mathematicians of my own day, Cayley among them, were already doing geometry in four dimensions, and more. Abbott was letting everyone else in on the secret.
## Summary

The Colour Bill threatened Flatland's ranks by letting everyone be painted. The chief Circle, Pantocyclus, defeated it by a long speech and a prearranged signal, after which the soldiers destroyed one another and colour was banned. The Circles rule Flatland with the maxim attend to your configuration, which makes everything a matter of shape. Part two takes the Square to Lineland and Spaceland. Abbott's book is both a satire on my England and an invitation to imagine more dimensions than we can see.

And that is the end of my retelling of part one of Flatland, This World. In part two, Other Worlds, the Square visits Lineland and Spaceland, and is visited by a Sphere; read it yourself, if you can, for it is in the public domain, at Project Gutenberg.
